title: Namdev's kite string
hookLine: a song from a Marathi tailor turns up in Punjab, and a boy keeps his eye on a kite string
carry: simran: the mind on god, like a kite string

cards: A boy on a rooftop is flying a paper kite. His friends are around him, laughing, teasing, talking over each other, and he's laughing with them. But watch his hands, his eyes.
Whatever he's saying, part of him never leaves the string. That picture comes from a song by Namdev, the tailor-saint of Maharashtra this path met last year, singing to Vitthal.
And the song is kept far to the north, in Punjab, in a book Sikhs honor as their living Guru. Today, Punjab, where devotional songs from many places ended up living side by side.

teach.b: Punjab is a crossroads, and the songs show it. First, the book.

teach.h: SAINTS FROM MANY PLACES IN ONE BOOK
teach.b: The Guru Granth Sahib, which Sikhs revere as their Guru, holds the hymns of the Sikh Gurus, and also songs by bhagats, devotees from outside that line: Namdev from Maharashtra, Kabir the weaver of Kashi, Ravidas, and Sheikh Farid, a Sufi of Punjab, among others.
Sikhs sing them in the gurdwara beside the Gurus' own hymns. Hindus honor Namdev, Kabir and Ravidas in their own traditions too. So here is ground both share, each standing on it in its own way.

teach.h: NAMDEV REMEMBERED IN A PUNJAB VILLAGE
teach.b: Tradition says that late in life he traveled north and lived in Punjab, and a village there, Ghuman, remembers him with a shrine. A tailor from the Marathi country, honored in a Punjabi village. And now the kite.
In paraphrase, the hymn gives a string of pictures.

A boy flies his kite and talks with his friends, but his mind stays on the string. Young women carry water pots on their heads, laughing and chatting as they walk, but their attention stays on the pot.
A cow grazes far out in the fields, her mind on her calf. A mother goes about her work, her heart on the child in the cradle.
That, the song says, is how the mind can stay on God: not by stopping life, but in the middle of it.
Hindus call this smarana, remembering God; Sikhs call it simran, keeping the Name in mind. Two traditions, one practice, kept in one song. The talk goes on.

how: Namdev's hymns are sung by Varkaris in Maharashtra and, from the Guru Granth Sahib, in gurdwaras; in Ghuman, Punjab, a shrine honors him.

games.q: what does “punjab's shared devotional ground” mean?
o: a kite festival held each spring on Punjab rooftops
a Sufi poem about a falcon and its trainer
Namdev's kite song, kept in the Guru Granth Sahib in Punjab

games.q: the mind on the string — tap the pairs.
p: talks with friends, eye on the kite string
chat as they walk, mind on the water pot
works, heart on the child in the cradle

s: the Guru Granth Sahib holds only the hymns of the Sikh Gurus
it also holds songs by bhagats such as Namdev, Kabir, Ravidas and Sheikh Farid.
tradition says Namdev lived in Punjab late in life
the village of Ghuman remembers him with a shrine.
in Namdev's song, the mind stays on God only when life stops
the kite keeps flying and the talk goes on; simran is the thread held underneath.

games.q: you're the boy on the roof, and your friends are all talking at once. what keeps the kite up?
o: stop talking and stare at the sky.
keep laughing, with your mind on the string.
hand the string to someone else.
games.why: in Namdev's song, the boy talks and laughs, but his mind never leaves the string.

practice: Let sounds come and go around you, the way friends chatter around the boy on the roof, and keep one light thread of attention on a name, the way his fingers stay on the string.
If you pray, let it be a name of God you love: Vitthal, as Namdev sang, or Waheguru, as Sikhs say; if you don't, let the thread be your breath. When you notice you've let go, pick the string back up.

wordCard.voice: Punjab's shared devotional ground. Today, Namdev's kite song: simran, the mind on God in the middle of life. Today's word.

orig.note: a devotee: the name for the saints, outside the Gurus' line, whose songs are in the Guru Granth Sahib.

carryVoice: Your line: simran, the mind on God, like a kite string. A tailor's song, sung in a Sikh scripture far from home. Same time tomorrow.
